utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madame, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-R.77.1, in the contempt case of Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. For the record, the accused is present in the courtroom, and so is his counsel, Ms. Isailovic. I understand, Ms. Isailovic, that you have got some preliminaries. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning [sic] President. Good morning -- good afternoon, Judges. First, a preliminary question, a motion under Article 73 or Rule 73 of the Regulation on the public character of court proceedings. Today, we came into the courtroom and the curtains -- the room was closed to the public. The curtains were down. And there are other factors impeding the access of the public to the proceedings. Your Court has made a ruling which was not notified to the Defence. Otherwise, the Defence would have responded to that motion that today's proceeding would be held in closed session. I realised that in today's schedule, it is said, "Closed session," but the number of the case was not mentioned; neither was the name of the accused, Mr. Dragan Jokic. I asked a question through the web site which publicizes the content of the court sessions, so through the internet, in other words, and they said that they had received that very schedule, and this prevented them from announcing today's session on the internet. Therefore, the general public has not been informed, hence all my colleagues. I'm wondering why I'm here today, and I'm also wondering if I can answer them, in view of this implicit order. Or this is the way I view it, because I have not been formally provided with such an order. Now, if you look at the Rules, at Rules 78 and 79, everything which is to do with the publicity of the proceedings is governed by those Rules. And if you look at Article 79, the principle of the publicity of the proceedings can be changed for reasons of public order or morality, safety, or non-disclosure of the identity of the victim and protection of the interests of the justice. Now, I wonder if such a factor exists, such a reason exists. And, anyway, whether we are working in open session or not today, the curtains are up now, I can see, but if you look at the matter of the fact of this, the curtains are up and the public cannot follow the debates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting a lot of precious time, Madame. Yes, the transcript has seized, anyway, the transcript has seized, so let's deal with that first. It's working now. Let me cut this short. You will recall for sure that there was one stage in the course of these proceedings, going back to the time when they had just started, then we had taken the decision that what was ex parte till then was to become public; namely, that contempt proceedings were instituted and were underway vis a vis or against your client. That was months ago. When we came to the evidentiary stage, I recall that precisely because we were asked by you and because of the details of the evidence that we were expecting or you were expecting, particularly on personal matters relating to your client, we decided that that evidence will be heard in closed session. So that evidence was heard in closed session, but essentially the proceedings themselves, namely, the contempt proceedings, are public proceedings. They have never been considered to be something secret, and they were never treated as something secret; nor are they going to be treated as something secret now. What will happen today is precisely what happened when you had your witnesses and when you brought over your expert and questions were put to your expert. In those occasions, we heard testimony in closed session, and that's what's going to happen today. So you don't need to worry, but of course until we start with the testimony, the session has to be in open session. And then as soon as the witness comes in and you start with your cross-examination, we go into closed session, and we will continue and finish in closed session unless there are reasons which would prompt you to ask that proceedings be conducted in open session. So I don't think I need to be more clear than I have been, and I think if you have got other preliminaries, you can move to your other preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge, and thank you for the suggestion, but I do still insist on my request. I had actually not finished, because you are saying that at any time I can ask for the proceedings to be held in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Stop one moment. The proceedings will be in closed session. They will be in open session only if you ask or if we decide that they no longer need to be in closed session. But otherwise, they will be -- your questions to the expert, to the psychiatrist, will be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is what I had understood. But the Rules are clear, so the Rule is public session, and the closed session is an exception to the Rule. So today we'll have a session for which the public was not informed, so de facto it will be a secret session, and the Defence opposes this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... waste time on these minutia. The public was informed there were going to be proceedings today. I agree with you that in the timetable or in the schedule, court schedule, the name of the case was not announced. That doesn't change a thing. It's open now. Everyone knows that the proceedings that are taking place now are against your client, so let's start, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I do not mean to show you any disrespect, but for me there is something serious going on. The principle of open sessions has been infringed, so I do persist and I would like to make a request under Article 73. I wanted to postpone the session and to summon another session at a -- for a later date, for which the public character would be secured and for which the public will be notified and informed about this session being held, or you can make a decision and notify it to the Defence under Article 79 of the Regulation. So whatever your decision will draw the consequences from it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we deliberate on this. Is it your intention to cross-examine the witness today, the psychiatrist appointed by the Trial Chamber, in closed session or in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My intention is to ask the majority of questions in public session. It's only those questions which are to do with the mental health of the client, but there will be very few of them, which, with your permission, will be in closed session and if you so decide it will be closed session. But the majority of the questions should be asked in public session, in my view, and this is why I am bothered by the fact that the public has not been warned of this session taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the whole of the ex-Yugoslavia will be waiting anxiously, gazing at their TV sets to see what this case is all about today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madame, the publicity requirement attaches to when the sitting takes place and not necessarily to the way the schedule of the Tribunal is announced. Anyone who is interested in knowing what is taking place today at the Tribunal will be able to follow these proceedings. The proceedings will be held in public, save when you need to -- need us to go into closed session, at which time we will go in closed session, as we did on previous occasions when you also had your own expert here. So anything else? This chapter is closed, so if you have any further preliminary submissions, speak now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since a part of the cross-examination will be highly technical, and since the expert report is partly very technical as well, I would need to call the Defence expert, Ms. Ana Najman, who appeared in court on the 10th of December last year, and for that purpose I would need to have a telephone line between 5.00 and 7.00 p.m. If you can plan the proceedings and breaks accordingly so that I can ask, if necessary, questions. I've already talked to my expert and warned her, but I would need a telephone because I'm not sitting in the office here and I don't have a protected line to talk to Ms. Najman. From the Defence room, it's impossible to make phone calls abroad, so I'd like to have this telephone line at some stage during about 20 minutes, so I ask the Chamber to order the services of the Tribunal to make a protected phone line available to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame, we were given advanced notice of this request of yours, and we were also informed that you were, in turn, informed by the administration here that you are paid administrative costs to cover such contingencies. So if you have the need to telephone or call your expert, this is your problem. You should make your own arrangements and not expect the Chamber to make them for you, nor I understand will the Registry be prepared to make these arrangements for you. That's number 1. Number 2 is this question of between 5.00 and 7.00 p.m. We will have a break as required, but it all depends on the time. It will all depend on where you will need -- when we will need the break. So let's start, and I think you have to find ways and means of contacting your expert, if you really need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's not a question of costs, because I'm willing to refund the costs of that telephone conversation using the expenses I receive from the Registry. The problem is I don't have a protected -- a secure telephone line, because I only have my mobile phone. So, technically, I do need a land line which is secure, and I will refund the expenses to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to sort this out with the Registry, not with us, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame, see if you can contact the Registrar and see if this can be arranged for Ms. Isailovic. Otherwise, we cannot involve ourselves in this. Anything else? Can we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final thing, Your Honour. How long do I have for the extra closing brief? You gave me four days, but I reserve the right, at the end of the closing brief, in view of the outcome of the proceedings, to apply for an extension of that deadline, which seems to me very short. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will tell us later on how much time you require, and we will adjust our decision accordingly. Let's bring the witness in, and we remain in open session for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness is brought in, I prepared copies of the reports. I don't know if you have copies of Mr. Vermetten's report and Ms. Najman's report, because I have prepared the copies and I can give them to Mr. Vermetten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We may need one copy for one of my colleagues, that's all, if you have one available. Good afternoon to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And a copy for the interpreters, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Good afternoon to you, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've summoned you here because we thought it would be in the interests of justice in this case that Madame Isailovic, who is appearing for the respondent, be given the opportunity to cross-examine you on the contents of your report and findings. So before you start giving evidence, our Rules would require from you that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. Please read out that statement, that declaration aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it you're comfortable giving evidence in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's great. Madame Isailovic, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vermetten. I'm Branislava Isailovic, attorney for Mr. Dragan Jokic, and I'm an attorney with the Paris Bar, but I will speak in B/C/S, the language spoked [sic] by accused, to just avoid much translation of your speech and mine. [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will distribute the copies -- I'll give the copies to Mr. Usher. These are the reports of Mr. Vermetten and of Mrs. Ana Najman. I will now ask Mr. Vermetten the following: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... hard copy of your -- yes. [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, I was just wondering if I should give Mr. Vermetten right away Ms. Najman's report, because I would like to ask him a few questions regarding that report. If you agree with this, with your permission, maybe Mr. Usher could hand him this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, of course, that would be very useful, and in the meantime perhaps, Mr. Vermetten, are you familiar with this report that had been prepared by Ms. Najman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume the report was just given me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, haven't been able read it, but I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, whether you're familiar with it, whether you've seen it for the first time today or whether you had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the first page, I have not seen this report before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As I have announced, Mr. Vermetten, I shall be asking questions in the B/C/S language, and I shall speak slowly in order to enable the interpreters to do their job and in order for Mr. Dragan Jokic to also be able to hear all the questions that I'm going to put to you. I should like to start with your CV, because unfortunately I did not have the honour of getting one and seeing what is this that you do and what your domain of expertise is, but I will ask you questions slowly and one by one. First of all, I should like to ask you about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: My educational background is: I studied medical school in University of Maastricht, after which I did a residency in psychiatry that I did in the Netherlands, partially, and in the Netherlands -- sorry, and in the United States, where I was further trained as a neuroscientist, before I returned back to the Netherlands in the year 2000, where I'm working as a psychiatrist and the head of a research department in the University Medical school at Utrecht.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I suggest something to you? If we were to make a distinction between the field or work in psychiatry, in psychology and as a neuropsychiatrist, a neurologist and a neuropsychologist, as far as I understood, you are a psychiatrist, that is where you put yourself, and a neurologist; right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: No, let me correct this. I am a psychiatrist. A psychiatrist in the Netherlands is somebody who has studied medical school, so he is a medical doctor, contrary to a psychologist, who has no medical license. So in addition to my medical license, I have a registration in the field of psychiatry, so that's four and a half years of specialisation in addition to medical school training. In addition to that, I studied the field of neuroscience, which is an open field for everybody, psychologists or psychiatrists and other related disciplines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me if I say that neuropsychology falls within a special separate domain of these neuropsychological sciences, and that for the work of a neuropsychologist, it is necessary for him to be specifically educated in order to be able to work in that field?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Well, it is so that a psychiatrist usually leans or lends his -- or gets his domain of expertise from various disciplines that can be from neurologists or psychologists, but it is not so that -- so I would say that psychiatry is a discipline that is integrating a lot of specialty fields. And in the old days we'd have in the Netherlands one specialty that covered neurology and psychiatry itself, doctor of nerve medicine or so, if you want to translate it, since about 20 years that has been disintegrated into a field of neurology and psychiatry. So it's the medical branch that studies issues that are related to the brain in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude that you have no training as a psychologist, then?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I wasn't trained as a psychologist, so let me answer that in that way. No. Can I add something, because that may be helpful. The field of psychology is dedicated to, where it is applicable, the normal health and normal behaviour of people that are sane, and where it leans to psychiatry, psychiatry is a field that deals with people who have some kind of illness, and the explanation for the illness needs to be taken from elements of other disciplines. So disease is the central item that we're dealing with, where the knowledge base might be helpful to get that from other fields, for instance, like neuropsychology or other related disciplines. Did I specify my question rightly for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all know the distinction between psychologists and psychiatrists, and that is one reason why we chose, as an expert, a psychiatrist and not a psychologist. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you do not analyse practically personality disorders, but just disease?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Well, personality disorder is also a disease in psychiatry, dealing a lot with personality disorders, so I would consider that, too, one of my expertises.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to enumerate exactly, as briefly as possible -- or, rather, to define exactly, as briefly as possible, the particular field of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Well, my field of expertise specialised in traumatic stress; that is to say, everything that is related to the exposure of stress or trauma, and you can differentiate that in severe violence, or war, or other domains where people are environmentally challenged, and the expertise of my field is to look at what that does to the human brain and the mind or the body and the mind, as that it compromises capacity. In the field ever since I left the Netherlands, I started to work with Vietnam veterans when I worked as a research associate at Yale University School of Medicine, where I looked at the effects of the Vietnam war on specific functions like health and disease, in particular, in people who are affected because of the Vietnam war, and that continued to be my special expertise. So my PhD that I did in university, in medical school, was about this issue. I did my PhD in the field of post-traumatic stress disorder, with the subtitle "Neurobiology and treatment," and I published extensively on this issue. I can give you all the references. Well, I could give you -- I think they are in my CV that I gave you, or that you might have a list of peer-reviewed journal articles that are on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since I never saw the CV of the witness, I believe that it would be very useful if we could have a copy of the said CV in order to continue in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can give her mine. She can have a look at it, and in the meantime then you can make a photocopy and you give her.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. This is very useful, in fact, for the proceedings. It would have been useful to get it before, but I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... surprised that you didn't have a copy. It's roughly three times or four times as long as the two reports put together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Better late than never, as one says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vermetten, I shall now like to deal with your experience as a court expert. Within the framework of your particular domain of expertise, what is your experience as a court expert? Is that also contained in the curriculum vitae, or can you refer me to that, or can you, yourself, give me a brief answer?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Let me try to define what a court expert is, if that means the cases in which I testified for court, I would assume so. That is not in my curriculum vitae. I have given two prior reports that started in the year 2008.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were those reports before this Chamber, this Court?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you are referring to some other cases, not this case, the Jokic case, but some other two cases in which you provided your expertise?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: One is the Jokic case, and the other one is another case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I noticed a mistake in the Jokic case, where another name, the name of somebody else, was revealed because it was contained in the Jokic report. It was from another case, but these things happen. But at any rate, that is your court experience, in terms of you giving your expertise before a tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's make this clear, because the interpretation that we got specifically makes reference "before a tribunal." I think you should give an answer which is much more comprehensive. As regards this Tribunal, you have already told us that this is the second time. In the Netherlands, before courts of law, for example, or outside the Netherlands, or inside the Netherlands but relating to other tribunals, have you ever had the opportunity to be a court-appointed expert or an expert appointed by some party during proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been a member of one additional moment. This was for the court in Arnhem and -- well as a psychiatric expert, I have been consultant, but not for a court in a situation like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I can sum up. So your experience as a court-appointed expert in your specific domain of your expertise that you have just defined would practically be confined to Jokic and to this other accused before the International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia, and this one case when you were a consultant in -- excuse my pronunciation if it is not good, Arnhem?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Correct, A-r-n-h-e-m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, to the best of my memory, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vermetten, I should now like to deal with another topic of my questioning which has to do with the circumstances of your appointment as expert, as a psychiatrist expert in the Jokic case, in which capacity you are also sitting here today. I, as Defence counsel, have been given two of your reports. Is that it, is this all that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Let me clear -- "I have been given two of your reports."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps it is not quite clear. Let me repeat. I, as Defence counsel for Dragan Jokic, have received one report that you submitted to the Registry of the Court on the 30th of May, a signed version, that is, and then unsigned version of the 29th of May, and I received another report which you submitted to the Registry on the 29th of July, current. Are these documents -- is that all that you submitted to the Registry in connection with your expert testimony in the Dragan Jokic case?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, before you started working on these reports, did you see any documents which have to do with the order of the Court for an expertise to be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer this question, the transcript doesn't show what your question [sic] was to the previous question -- what your answer was to the previous question. The previous question was as follows, referring to the two reports: "Are these documents -- is that all you submitted to the Registry in connection with your expert testimony in the Dragan Jokic case?" Did you submit anything else, apart from those two reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that formulation, the answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's okay, let's proceed. We've got it clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe there's a slight confusion here, because you've rephrased the question in a different way, because the initial answer was, "Yes," but now it's, "No."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clear. Don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vermetten, my next question was whether you had occasion to see Court orders whereby the examination of the accused in the Dragan Jokic case was actually instructed to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think in the question that was addressed to me to perform my expertise, I was given this information sent by somebody from The Hague, who invited me to be the expert, so the answer is "yes," but I don't know how specific your referring to that information was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me be clear. Do you recall that someone asked you for the first time to, as soon as possible, state your -- [In English] [Previous translation continues]... "up to and after the service of subpoena on him"?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I'm trying to read the script here on the monitor, but I was asked to give a psychiatric expertise on the case, so that I did and was my report that you're referring to was dated the 29th of March, with an accompanying letter of March the 30th. And then later I was asked again with a specific question; that I was asked to revisit Mr. Jokic for a specific question that I addressed in my report on July 29. So the first was rather general, a psychiatric evaluation, and the second one was specific regarding a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there were two questions the second time?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Not exactly. I'm reading it aloud, and I'm giving answer to those two questions in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me who it was that you got in touch the first time, when you were asked to make a general psychiatric assessment of Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: The name of the person who contacted me for that or --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I'm more interested to what particular body of this Tribunal that person belonged. You can also give me the name. I believe that there is no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because obviously you can't put direct questions, while we can. From the moment you were approached to undertake this task, who did you deal with? Did you deal with the Judges or did you deal with members of the Registry and members of the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And whom did you give the report to, the two reports, when they were ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have sent the report to (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I may have c.c.'ed it, too, in reverse order, but according to his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you got these two specific questions after your first report, did anyone explain to you why that was and what the difference, practically, was between these two reports?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Well, the questions were pretty much self-explanatory, that these were the specific issues that needed to be dealt with that a report, as such, didn't give an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in the first question, and I have the court order here before me, you were supposed to reply to -- or, rather, I shall read it in English, the decision, that is: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... appoint him or her to examine Jokic in accordance with professional practice and to report to the Trial Chamber as soon as possible on the mental condition of Jokic prior to and after the service of the subpoena on him." [Interpretation] And after that, you got a second question, and I insist on the second because there were two; namely, that you were to state your opinion, [in English] "His," [Interpretation], meaning Dragan Jokic, [Previous translation continues]... [in English] "in mind when he refused to testify in Prosecutor vs. Popovic et al." [Interpretation] My question as a layperson is the following: How did you personally perceive the difference between you specifying the mental condition in the first case, which you did, and in the second case defined his state of mind? Please clarify for us what the difference is and how you perceive that difference.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Our profession is really difficult in this case, to report on the mental condition that somebody was where the psychiatrist in consultation was not present, so in retrospect to judge about that is really a difficult one. So you can rather only be circumstantial and find circumstantial evidence to prior reports or psychiatric consultations were by others to build a construct of what could have likely been the case. And I understood or maybe that was the interpretation of the people who read this, that they would try to formulate the questions so as to be more specific that they could help the Court to narrow it down. So, therefore, I took it as a normal sequence of events, that they would try to get more specific information on this issue -- on these issues that were asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Later, I shall dwell more on the substance of the report itself. But if I can summarise, it was quite clear to you why they first asked for this one assessment, which to me, as a layperson, is almost identical to this other assessment, and why later they asked you for this different second opinion which was formulated as a specific question put to you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Nothing is quite clear, but this was clear enough for me to take it on and to reply to the question that was asked with more specificity than I could in relation to the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Vermetten, in your expertise in assessing the state of mind or the traumatic stress experienced by a person and how that affected human capacities, you actually gave that expertise by submitting your first report, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to move on to your methodology of work. This is the kind of questions that we also asked the previous expert, and I believe that to be very useful. Firstly, I'm not quite clear. From your reports, I guess that there were three visits to Dragan Jokic, but regrettably I could not find in your report the date of the third visit. So please kindly tell us how many visits were there and when.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I think in my report, in the first report -- for the first report, I visited Mr. Jokic on two occasions; April 15 for two and a half hours, and April 22nd for two hours at the Detention Unit. And for the second report, I visited Mr. Jokic once on -- let me see where it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is not written there. That is why I'm asking you. Perhaps you have it in one of your notebooks.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't read it here in the -- in the second report, so I must have it somewhere in my notebook. I'm sorry that that wasn't clearly stated in the report, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you do assert that you were there for a third time?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Definitely, yes, and I can say the duration was about the same; about two, two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me now who was present during these examinations.

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember their names, but every -- every visit, I was accompanied by a translator for the whole duration of that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I then conclude that these examinations took place with the aid of an interpreter, that you did not communicate directly with Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Well, let me rephrase that. We communicated by verbal as well as non-verbal behaviour. But the verbal part, yes, I could only -- I know a little bit of Serbian, let's say, but I was helped by the translator.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to assess now what was the portion of the participation of the interpreter in these six and a half or seven hours that you spent there, how would you apportion this period to interpretation, because as I understand it, you put a question, then an interpreter translates it to Jokic, Jokic answers it, and then the answer is interpreted back to you. Was that how this communication went?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Correct. I must then say there was a -- I had the opportunity to continuously observe the verbal and non-verbal behaviour of Mr. Jokic all through the time, as well he responded or not responded. Let me be clear. In the profession, it's important also to look at somebody when he's silent and not saying anything. So both accounts. But let me put a figure. The speech was rather slow, because at times it was difficult to grasp the material that was asked. So it's roughly to put a percentage, but 40 per cent -- no, more than that. So it's the same as here. When you communicate, there are pauses and silences, and I don't know whether actually everything is translated well. And sometimes when it gets emotional, you have to go back to the issue, which therefore can take quite -- consume quite some time before I'm confident and satisfied with the answer that I was -- that to me was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify to me what you mean when you say "satisfied"? In what sense?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: In the sense that I could sort of sum up all the observations that I have made over that period of time. So the -- let me say -- so the advantage of having been able to examine somebody on two prior visits surely definitely facilitated me in my third -- in my third visit to Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this particular point in time, I would like to request something. I realised that in the evidence 7A and 7B, in those reports, and those are the reports of Ms. Ana Najman, I've noticed a mistake in the translation regarding -- it's actually on page 55 of our file. The mistake regards the time that Ms. Ana Najman spent with Mr. Jokic. In the original, we can read that she examined him for two days, five hours a day, whereas in the English version we can read that she spent five hours all together with him. So that's actually half of the time spent with him in reality, so I would kindly request that you order a modification or correction of this mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll take judicial notice of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vermetten, in your report, at the very beginning, make references to certain documents that you had used, and also to some persons that you had consulted during drafting your reports for the Chamber, and I can read that now. We can read it together, actually. So in your first report, you make reference to the consultation with Dr. -- I think the name is Vera Petrovic, Mr. Jokic's psychiatrist. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then a neuropsychiatric report prepared by Dr. Vera Petrovic, submitted by her on the 22nd of April, 2008; then a communication with -- and I may mispronounce this name, that's Ms. Remelzvan [phoen], a nurse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Madame, because our attention is being drawn to the fact that a witness's report is confidential, was filed by the Registrar confidential. Now, you're making a specific reference to parts of the same report, or one of them, for the time being in open session, so there are two options. We either go into private session or closed session, when you are making specific references to the report, or I consult with my colleagues whether they are prepared to lift the confidentiality at least for the purpose of these questions. But I don't know what the follow-up questions will be, so I would be hesitant in lifting the confidentiality; I, personally. I mean, I don't know what my colleagues would do. Let me consult them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If your client is prepared to lift the confidentiality, then we can proceed in open session; lift the confidentiality of the report, obviously, for the purposes of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that the questions that concern the methodology of the work of the expert do not fall within the realm of confidentiality. But just to reassure you, I will reformulate my question; that is, that I will put direct questions, because it doesn't concern the content of the report but precisely the method of work, and I will just put the question to the expert and have him answer on the basis of what he referred in drafting his report. Aside from the examination of Mr. Jokic, of course all the data concerning the mental health and Mr. Jokic's family, of course, should remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine with us. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vermetten, you have understood what the problem was. I would just like you to remind yourself on what basis, apart from the examination of Mr. Jokic, you drafted your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: So it is in the first report, on page number 3, and I don't think I have to read it aloud, but you were commencing on the consultations that I had made prior to my first visit of Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to explain it to you now. Please, do not mention the report. I'm only interested in this as the methodology of your work. Whether it is written in the report or not, we know about that. And just to avoid going into private session, please tell me that, and you can just explain to me what else you did, apart from examining Mr. Dragan Jokic; who you talked to, what materials you read, without going into what they told you. Please just tell me, who did you communicate with prior to drawing up your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I had a consultation with his treating psychiatrist or the psychiatrist that had known him from the past by e-mail, and I requested permission by Mr. Jokic to consult. I don't know whether I did that after my -- I must hesitate. Usually, I do that, and I think I did it in this case also, that I requested -- yes, I requested permission to consult this person, after my first visit, to -- one way to corroborate what was told, whether that was true, and then to request additional information, since there were no neuropsychiatric reports that I could use in my report. So that was a source of information, right, so a part was, as it says, the consultation, part was the neuropsychiatric report, and to -- since there was medication involved in the treatment of Mr. Jokic, and there was no record of when -- what medication was, and I know that some medication may impair somebody's capacity to judge or his mental capacity can be impaired because of a compromised function by medication, I wanted to know at what time what medication was prescribed for what. And since some medication had started, I needed to have that, which I learned was quite unusual. But I thought it was essential for me to have that information, and therefore I consulted with the unit nurses that were available to me at that time. And then the third part of information, but this is just for general information, is there is a web site where I could contextualise the information about the case and about the further procedures and situation of the procedure of this Court, so the web site that I referred to in the report was also a valuable database for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me stick to your first report. You say here, [Previous translation continues]... which I learned was quite unusual. Could you please clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to explain, because I, for myself, did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: While you were answering my previous answer [as interpreted], and I'm reading from the transcript, that was how it was translated, line 18, you can see it yourself: "I needed to have that, which I learned was quite unusual." And I would kindly ask you to explain to us why was that what you received unusual?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: I learned that Mr. Jokic was given either the Bromazepam or some medicine that had started on a specific day, and I wanted to know prior to giving this, if you give somebody a certain medication, there needs to be something you give it for, so what was the incident that was -- happened prior before. And since I didn't have a medical record, my usual practice, how I do that with patients, is go to other charts. And what I learned from the research nurses and the unofficial part is that they say, "Oh, we don't get a lot of requests for -- for this." So it may not be necessary by other consultants before to have that information, but in this specific occasion I thought it was important for me to have that information. And I was referring to one of the quotes that the nurses made when I asked permission to look into the medical chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We have these medical documents as part of the case file, and we have already commented on this with Ana Najman, the expert. When you were preparing your second report, did you rely on any additional information as well?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: No. For my second report, I only relied on information -- since I already had access to enough information for the first report, I could base my report on the interview that I had with him for that single visit, and it was not essential or needed -- necessary for me to spend another visit or request additional information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC VERMETTEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. You said, "Did you rely on any additional information?" I said, "No, I relied on the information that was in the second visit. That was sufficient for me."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because I'd like to refer to the content of the report, I would therefore ask you if we could move to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Madame, how much time do you require for your additional brief?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least ten days, because I have other commitments with my law firm in Paris. Let me just explain things to you. This is even more important for me than the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are giving you more than that. We are giving you up to the end of the recess, that is, up to the 12th of January. That should be ample time for you to present us with your additional Defence brief, final brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I also want to take this opportunity to wish you the very best for the festive season, Madame. Thank you. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame, before we rise, would you like to consult with your client and ask him whether he wishes to make any further statements? Actually, he has heard us. Mr. -- no, he doesn't wish to make further statements. I saw him. All right, thank you. So we stand adjourned. We'll wait for your final brief, and then we will come down with our judgement in due course. Thank you.
